questiontext.text: What problem does external merge sort primarily solve?

answer.text: Sorting a dataset that is too large to fit entirely in main memory (RAM)

feedback.text: Correct — the data lives on disk and cannot be held in RAM all at once.

answer.text: Sorting an array faster than O(n log n) comparisons

feedback.text: No — it does not beat the comparison lower bound; it manages data that exceeds RAM.

answer.text: Removing duplicate keys from a small in-memory list

feedback.text: No — deduplication is not the point; the problem is scale beyond memory.

answer.text: Sorting linked lists without extra pointers

feedback.text: No — that is unrelated to external sorting.

generalfeedback.text: External sorting handles data too large for RAM by streaming it between memory and disk in sorted pieces.

questiontext.text: What dominates the running time of external merge sort?

answer.text: Disk I/O — the number of passes made over the data

feedback.text: Correct — moving data to and from disk is far slower than in-memory comparisons.

answer.text: The number of key comparisons performed by the CPU

feedback.text: No — CPU comparisons are cheap relative to disk transfers here.

answer.text: The recursion stack depth

feedback.text: No — stack depth is not the bottleneck for external sorting.

answer.text: The number of pivot selections

feedback.text: No — pivots belong to quicksort, not external merge sort.

generalfeedback.text: Because disk access is orders of magnitude slower than memory, the cost model counts passes / I/O, not comparisons.

questiontext.text: Which best describes the first phase (run creation) of external merge sort?

answer.text: Read chunks that fit in memory, sort each internally, and write them back as sorted "runs"

feedback.text: Correct — each memory-sized chunk becomes one sorted run on disk.

answer.text: Merge all runs at once into the final sorted output

feedback.text: No — that is the second (merge) phase.

answer.text: Partition the data around a pivot chosen from disk

feedback.text: No — external merge sort does not partition around pivots.

answer.text: Build a heap over the entire file in memory

feedback.text: No — the whole file does not fit in memory; only chunks do.

generalfeedback.text: Phase 1 produces sorted runs; phase 2 repeatedly k-way-merges those runs until one remains.

questiontext.text: Using a (B−1)-way merge, how does increasing the merge order (fan-in k) affect the number of merge passes, roughly ⌈logk(N/M)⌉?

answer.text: Larger k means fewer passes, so less total disk I/O

feedback.text: Correct — a higher fan-in raises the logarithm base, shrinking the pass count.

answer.text: Larger k means more passes and more I/O

feedback.text: No — a bigger merge order reduces the number of passes.

answer.text: k has no effect on the number of passes

feedback.text: No — k is the logarithm base, so it directly changes the pass count.

answer.text: Passes depend only on CPU speed, not k

feedback.text: No — passes depend on N, M, and the fan-in k, not CPU speed.

generalfeedback.text: Number of merge passes ≈ ⌈logk(N/M)⌉; each pass moves ≈ 2N records, so higher k lowers both passes and I/O.

questiontext.text: External merge sort, like ordinary merge sort, can be implemented as a stable sort.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — a careful merge preserves the relative order of equal keys.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: No — merging can keep equal keys in their original order, so it is stable.

questiontext.text: For a file far larger than RAM, the number of CPU key comparisons is the main bottleneck of external merge sort.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — disk I/O (passes over the data), not comparisons, dominates.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — disk passes dominate; comparisons are comparatively cheap.

questiontext.text: A sorted chunk written to disk during phase 1, later combined by merging, is called a ______.

answer.text: run

feedback.text: Correct — these sorted pieces are called runs.

answer.text: run*

feedback.text: Correct — a sorted "run".

answer.text: sorted run

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which changes reduce the number of passes (and thus disk I/O) in external merge sort? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Giving the sort more memory M so each initial run is longer

feedback.text: Yes — larger runs mean fewer runs to merge, so fewer passes.

answer.text: Increasing the merge fan-in k (a higher-order merge)

feedback.text: Yes — a larger k raises the log base and cuts the pass count.

answer.text: Using a smaller memory buffer to save RAM

feedback.text: No — less memory yields shorter runs and more passes.

answer.text: Performing more CPU comparisons per record

feedback.text: No — extra comparisons do not reduce disk passes.

generalfeedback.text: Fewer passes come from bigger memory (longer runs) and higher merge order; both attack the ⌈logk(N/M)⌉ pass count.
